title: A2 Review: Small Words That Carry a Lot
subtitle: Prepositions, quantifiers and comparatives — the parts of English that look easy and are not.
description: An A2 review reading and listening text on prepositions, some/any/no, much/many and comparative forms, with practice exercises on each.
passage: The hardest words in English are not the long ones. They are the short ones, and there are three groups of them that give trouble at this level.

First, prepositions of place. The rough rule is that IN is for something enclosed — in a bag, in a room, in New York — ON is for a surface — on the table, on the wall, on the floor — and AT is for a point rather than a space: at the door, at the airport, at the bus stop. The same three words do time as well, and the pattern is similar: IN a month or a year, ON a day, AT a clock time. In June, on Monday, at eight o'clock. There is no logic to learn beyond that, and the only way to fix it is to meet the phrases often enough that the wrong one starts to sound wrong.
A few more are worth having: THROUGH for going in one side and out the other, BETWEEN for two things, AMONG for many, INTO for movement to the inside, and UNDER for underneath.

Second, the quantifiers. English divides nouns into two kinds and treats them differently, which most languages do not. You can count chairs, eggs and questions, so they take MANY and A FEW. You cannot count milk, money, time or information, so they take MUCH and A LITTLE. “How many eggs?” but “How much milk?” Get this wrong and everybody still understands you, which is exactly why it is so easy to keep getting it wrong for years.

There is also a small difference that matters more than its size suggests. A FEW and A LITTLE are positive: I have a few friends here means you are not alone. FEW and LITTLE without the article are negative: I have few friends here means you are lonely. One small word changes the meaning of the sentence completely.

SOME, ANY and NO follow their own pattern. SOME goes in positive sentences — I have some questions — and also in offers and requests, which is the exception: Would you like some coffee? ANY goes in negatives and questions: I do not have any questions. Is there any milk? NO replaces “not any”: There is no milk, which means the same as there is not any milk but is shorter and stronger.

Third, comparatives. Short words add -ER and -EST: cheap, cheaper, the cheapest. Long words take MORE and THE MOST: expensive, more expensive, the most expensive. The dividing line is roughly two syllables, and the usual mistake is to do both at once — “more cheaper” is the single most common error at this level. And the irregular ones have to be learned: good, better, the best; bad, worse, the worst; far, further, the furthest.

vocabulary.definition: the flat outside part of something
a word showing how much or how many, such as some or many
to say how many there are
when you ask somebody if they would like something

exercises.title: In, On, At and a Few More
exercises.instructions: Enclosed space, surface, or point? Then the same three for time.

items.prompt: The keys are ___ my bag and the picture is ___ the wall.
items.explanation: A bag encloses; a wall is a surface.

items.prompt: She arrived ___ the airport ___ eight o'clock.
items.explanation: An airport is treated as a point on a journey, and clock times always take at.

items.prompt: I will meet you ___ Monday, and my birthday is ___ June.
items.explanation: On for days, in for months and years.

items.prompt: We walked ___ the park and the dog ran ___ the house.
items.explanation: Through means in one side and out the other; into is movement to the inside.

items.prompt: He is sitting ___ me and John, and the cat is ___ the table.
items.explanation: Between is for two, among for many. Under means underneath.

items.prompt: She lives ___ New York and he is waiting ___ the bus stop.
items.explanation: A city encloses you; a bus stop is a point. Note that you are ON the bus itself.

exercises.title: Much, Many, Some, Any
exercises.instructions: Can you count it? And is the sentence positive, negative or a question?

items.prompt: How ___ milk do you need? Not ___ — just a little.
items.explanation: Milk cannot be counted, so much in both places.
Eggs can be counted: many and a few.

items.prompt: I have ___ questions about the homework.
Is there ___ milk? No, there is ___ milk at all.
items.explanation: Any in the question; no replaces “not any” and is shorter and stronger.
The exception: offers and requests take some even though they are questions.

items.prompt: She has ___ ___ friends here, so she is often lonely.
items.explanation: Few without “a” is negative. “A few friends” would mean she is not alone at all.

exercises.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
exercises.instructions: Short word or long word? And never both forms at once.

items.prompt: This bag is ___ than that one.
items.explanation: Cheap is short, so -er. “More cheaper” is the most common error at this level.

items.prompt: This restaurant is ___ ___ than the other one.
items.explanation: Expensive has three syllables, so it takes more.

items.prompt: It was ___ film I have ever seen — I loved it.
items.explanation: Good → better → the best. Irregular, and has to be learned.

items.prompt: The traffic today is ___ than yesterday.
This is ___ ___ interesting book on the list.
items.explanation: The superlative of a long word: the most + adjective. The “the” is not optional.

discussion: Describe your room using six prepositions of place.
“I have a few friends here” and “I have few friends here” mean different things. Does your own language make that distinction?
Which countable/uncountable pairs catch you out? (Information, advice, news and furniture are the usual ones.)
Compare three places you have lived or visited, using a comparative and a superlative.
Write about 100 words comparing two cities, using at least three comparatives and one superlative.
